10.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what do you ask a foot and ankle patient?"
- "Pain, deformity, instability, swelling, stiffness and pins and needles."
- "Shoes, walking distance, work and sport; then diabetes, rheumatoid disease and the spine."

### Pain — where and when
| Site | Think of |
|---|---|
| Front of the ankle | arthritis with impingement |
| Sinus tarsi | subtalar joint |
| Behind the medial malleolus | tibialis posterior tendon |
| Behind the lateral malleolus | peroneal tendons |
| Back of the heel | Achilles insertion, Haglund bump |
| Under the heel, first steps | plantar fasciitis |
| Between metatarsal heads, burning | Morton's neuroma |
| Diffuse burning sole | tarsal tunnel syndrome |

| Clue | Points to |
|---|---|
| Worse going upstairs | anterior impingement |
| Worse going downstairs | posterior impingement |
| Worse on uneven ground | subtalar joint, peroneal tendons |
| Better in a brace | instability |

- **Memory:** up the stairs = front; down the stairs = back (Nagah)

### Instability, deformity, swelling
- Instability: recurrent sprains, "giving way" on uneven ground
- Deformity: arch "going over", bunion, toes rubbing in shoes
- Swelling: painless diabetic foot → Charcot; both feet → systemic

#### Ask every time
| Complaint | Ask |
|---|---|
| Pain | site, weight bearing, night |
| Function | walking distance, shoes, work, sport |
| Past | trauma, operations, steroid injections |
| General | diabetes, rheumatoid, gout, neurology |
| Spine | back pain; many foot deformities are neurological |

- **Red flags:** night pain, fever, painless hot swollen foot
- **Memory:** two P's, two S's, I and D — pain, pins and needles, swelling, stiffness, instability, deformity
- General interview → ch 1

10.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "examine this foot and ankle"
- "Standing: look from front, side and back; tiptoe on both, then one foot."
- "Walking: gait, toes, heels. Sitting: soles and shoes."
- "Supine: feel, move each joint, power, sensation, pulses; then spine and knee."

- **Whole foot and ankle exam (video):** [▶ Dr James Gill · 7:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2nVv0Xnt0l0)

### The route on one page
| Position | What you do (in order) |
|---|---|
| Standing | Look: front, side, back · heel, arches, too-many-toes |
| Standing | Special: heel rises, Jack test, Coleman block |
| Walking | gait; toes, heels, outer and inner borders |
| Sitting | soles, between the toes; shoes |
| Supine | Feel: medial, front, lateral, back, sole · pulses |
| Sitting or supine | Move: ankle, subtalar, midtarsal, first MTP · Silfverskiöld |
| Sitting | Special: drawer, tilt, squeeze, rotation, Mulder, Tinel |
| Prone → Finish | Thompson, Matles · neurology · spine, knee |

- MTP = metatarsophalangeal joint
- **Memory:** in each position Look, Feel, Move, Special; then Neuro, Vascular, Joints
- Expose both legs from mid-thigh, shoes and socks off

### Standing
#### Look — front, side, back
| View | Look for |
|---|---|
| Front | ankle swelling, toes, nails, skin |
| Side | medial arch: flat (planus) or high (cavus) |
| Back | heel alignment, calf wasting, Achilles, too-many-toes |

- Describe deformity back to front: hindfoot, midfoot, forefoot, toes (Nagah)
- From behind, check the spine: hairy patch, dimple, sinus
- Normal heel: 5–10° valgus to the calf (Reider)

[[FIG: Fig 10.1 — Three views; valgus and varus heel · 10.02

#### Special — heel rise and flexibility
- Tiptoe on both feet, then one (10.4)
- Flat foot → Jack test; cavus → Coleman block (10.3)

### Walking
| Gait | What you see |
|---|---|
| **Stiff big toe** | rolls off the outer border, no push-off |
| **Equinus** | leg turned out, early heel rise |

- Antalgic, drop-foot and short-limb gaits → ch 1 (1.3)

| Walk on | Tests |
|---|---|
| Toes | calf (gastrocnemius–soleus), S1 |
| Heels | tibialis anterior, L4 |
| Outer border | invertors (tibialis posterior) |
| Inner border | evertors (peronei) |

- **Memory:** toes = calf; heels = front; outer border = invertors; inner = evertors

[[FIG: Fig 10.2 — Walking on toes, heels and borders · 10.02

### Sitting — soles and shoes
- Look at the sole and between the toes: callus, ulcer, corns
- Diabetic ulcers: first metatarsal head, hallux pulp, second and third heads

[[FIG: Fig 10.3 — Callosities show only when you turn the foot · 10.02

| Shoe sign | Points to |
|---|---|
| Inner sole worn, upper bulging in | flat foot |
| Worn under metatarsal heads and heel | cavus foot |
| Bulge over the bunion | hallux valgus |
| Oblique toe-box crease | hallux rigidus |

[[FIG: Fig 10.4 — Shoe wear patterns · 10.02

### Supine — feel
- The foot is superficial: the tender spot names the structure

| Side | Feel |
|---|---|
| Medial | deltoid, tibialis posterior, tarsal tunnel, navicular |
| Front | tendons, joint line, dorsalis pedis |
| Lateral | ATFL, CFL, sinus tarsi, peronei, fifth metatarsal |
| Back | Achilles, retrocalcaneal bursa, Haglund bump |
| Sole | fascia origin, metatarsal heads, sesamoids |

- ATFL = anterior talofibular ligament; CFL = calcaneofibular ligament
- **Memory:** behind the medial malleolus, front to back — "Tom, Dick and Harry": tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum, (artery, nerve), flexor hallucis (Hoppenfeld)

[[FIG: Fig 10.5 — Structures to feel; tendons behind the malleolus · 10.02
[[FIG: Fig 10.6 — Sinus tarsi tenderness; foot pulses · 10.02

### Supine or sitting — move
| Joint (Nagah) | Normal |
|---|---|
| Ankle dorsiflexion / plantarflexion | 20° / 50° |
| Subtalar inversion / eversion | about 20° / 10° (Exam Techniques) |
| Forefoot adduction / abduction | 5° each |
| First MTP dorsiflexion / plantarflexion | 70° / 40° |

- **Memory:** ankle 20–50, big toe 70–40; inversion twice eversion

| Joint | How to hold |
|---|---|
| Ankle | invert the heel to lock the subtalar joint |
| Subtalar | hold the talus; tilt the heel in and out |
| Midtarsal | fix the heel; move the forefoot |

[[FIG: Fig 10.7 — Ankle, subtalar, first MTP · 10.02

| Lost dorsiflexion from | Clue |
|---|---|
| Joint | arthritis, painful crepitus |
| Front | osteophytes or synovium (impingement) |
| Calf | tight gastrocnemius (Silfverskiöld, 10.3) |
| Syndesmosis | scarred after sprain or fracture |

### Finish — neuro, vascular, joints
| Muscle (MRC grade) | Test |
|---|---|
| Tibialis posterior | plantarflexed foot, resisted inversion |
| Tibialis anterior | dorsiflexed, inverted foot; resist plantarflexion |
| Peronei | plantarflexed, everted foot; resist inversion |
| Calf | 10 single heel rises = grade 5 (Reider) |

- Sensation: L4 medial, L5 dorsum, S1 lateral border and sole (Nagah)
- Ankle reflex S1; Babinski, clonus; roots → ch 9, nerves → ch 5
- Pulses: dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial; then knee and lumbar spine

[[FIG: Fig 10.8 — Power of the three tendons · 10.02
[[FIG: Fig 10.9 — L4, L5, S1 skin; ankle reflex · 10.02

PITFALL — "examining a cavus foot without the spine"
- Cavovarus is often neurological: Charcot–Marie–Tooth, spinal dysraphism, cord tumour (Exam Techniques)
- Say → "**I would examine the spine, the hands and the neurology.**"

10.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "is this deformity flexible?"
- "Flat foot: Jack test and tiptoe — arch forms, heel inverts = flexible."
- "Cavus foot: Coleman block — heel corrects = hindfoot flexible."
- "Tight calf: Silfverskiöld — gastrocnemius or tendo-Achilles."

### Flat foot (pes planus)
- Three parts: heel valgus, flat medial arch, forefoot abduction (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- Ask two things: flexible or rigid? One side or both?
- Flexible: arch returns off weight, on tiptoe, with big-toe extension

| Rigid flat foot | Clue |
|---|---|
| Tarsal coalition | young, fixed valgus, peroneal spasm |
| Tibialis posterior, late | adult, one side, cannot rise on tiptoe |
| Inflammatory arthritis | other joints, both feet |

- **Memory:** rigid flat foot in the young = coalition until proved otherwise

[[FIG: Fig 10.10 — Cavus and planus; course flat foot · 10.03
[[FIG: Fig 10.11 — Supple foot arches off weight; rigid stays flat · 10.03

#### Jack test
- **Aim:** flexible or rigid flat foot
- **How:** patient stands; you extend the big toe passively
- **Positive:** arch forms → flexible; stays flat → rigid
- **Why:** windlass — the plantar fascia tightens and lifts the arch
- **Video:** [▶ Global HELP · 1:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R1AGYMt329k)

[[FIG: Fig 10.12 — Big toe extended, arch rises · 10.03

#### Double heel rise (tiptoe) test
- **Aim:** flexibility of the flat foot
- **How:** patient rises on both tiptoes; you watch the heels from behind
- **Positive:** heel turns into varus → flexible; stays in valgus → rigid
- **Why:** needs a mobile subtalar joint and a working tibialis posterior
- **Video:** [▶ Global HELP · 0:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nolevVWzdio)

[[FIG: Fig 10.13 — Heels invert on tiptoe · 10.03

### Cavus foot (pes cavus)
- Three parts: heel varus, high arch, plantarflexed first ray (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- Both feet → Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease (CMT), the commonest; one foot → spinal dysraphism
- Look at the hands for intrinsic wasting and clawing

#### Coleman block test
- **Aim:** is the heel varus fixed or flexible?
- **How:** patient stands on a block under heel and lateral foot; first ray hangs free
- **Positive:** heel corrects to valgus → flexible, forefoot-driven; stays varus → fixed
- **Why:** the plantarflexed first ray forces the heel into varus
- **Video:** [▶ Global HELP · 1:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TCp25F0l7hc)

[[FIG: Fig 10.14 — First ray off the block edge · 10.03

### Big toe
| | Hallux valgus | Hallux rigidus |
|---|---|---|
| Look | toe drifts out, bunion | dorsal bump over first MTP |
| Move | range kept, often correctable | dorsiflexion lost and painful |
| Gait | pain in shoes | no push-off; rolls outward |

- Hallux valgus: check toe pronation and second-toe crowding
- Hallux valgus angle normal <15°; intermetatarsal angle <9° (Miller)

[[FIG: Fig 10.15 — Hallux valgus and rigidus · 10.03

### Lesser toes
| Toe | Deformity |
|---|---|
| Mallet | flexed DIP joint |
| Hammer | flexed PIP joint |
| Claw | extended MTP, flexed PIP and DIP |

- PIP = proximal interphalangeal; DIP = distal interphalangeal
- **Memory:** mallet at the tip, hammer in the middle, claw up at the base
- Flexible? Push the metatarsal heads up; the PIP straightens

[[FIG: Fig 10.16 — Hammer, claw and mallet toes · 10.03

### Is the calf tight?
#### Silfverskiöld test
- **Aim:** tight gastrocnemius or tight tendo-Achilles
- **How:** invert the heel to lock the midtarsal joint; dorsiflex, knee straight then bent 90°
- **Positive:** more dorsiflexion with knee bent → gastrocnemius; no change → tendo-Achilles
- **Why:** gastrocnemius crosses the knee; soleus does not
- **Trap:** midtarsal not locked → the midfoot fakes dorsiflexion (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- **Video:** [▶ Global HELP · 4:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=La9LUJwGGQ0)

[[FIG: Fig 10.17 — Knee straight, then bent · 10.03

| Result | Surgery (Kasr Al-Ainy) |
|---|---|
| Better with knee bent | gastrocnemius recession |
| Same in both | tendo-Achilles lengthening |

PITFALL — "calling a flat foot flexible because it looks mild"
- Prove it: arch with Jack test, heel inversion on tiptoe
- Say → "**The arch reforms and the heel inverts on tiptoe, so the deformity is flexible.**"

10.04.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "the key foot tests"
- "Achilles: Thompson. Tibialis posterior: single heel rise. Lateral ligament: drawer and tilt."
- "Syndesmosis: squeeze and external rotation. Forefoot: Mulder. Tarsal tunnel: Tinel."

### Is the Achilles ruptured?
#### Thompson (Simmonds) test
- **Aim:** complete Achilles rupture
- **How:** patient prone, feet over the couch end; you squeeze the calf
- **Positive:** no plantarflexion → complete rupture
- **Why:** squeezing the calf pulls an intact tendon
- **Trap:** a partial tear still plantarflexes
- **Video:** [▶ AMBOSS · 1:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xFnWAjrTGHc)

[[FIG: Fig 10.18 — Calf squeezed, foot plantarflexes if intact · 10.04

#### Matles test
- **Aim:** Achilles rupture
- **How:** patient prone, knees flexed actively to 90°; you watch the feet
- **Positive:** foot falls to neutral or dorsiflexion → rupture (Campbell)
- **Why:** lost resting tension; the sound foot stays plantarflexed
- **Video:** [▶ Sports Med Review · 0:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kUSxECkY0xc)

[[FIG: Fig 10.19 — Affected foot drops to neutral · 10.04

### Is tibialis posterior working?
#### Too-many-toes sign
- **Aim:** forefoot abduction in flat foot
- **How:** patient stands; you look from behind at both feet
- **Positive:** more than about 1.5 toes, or than the sound side → abducted forefoot (Exam Techniques)
- **Why:** the abducted forefoot shows lateral to the heel
- **Video:** [▶ Sports Med Review · 1:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kkCRIGKgqHM)

[[FIG: Fig 10.20 — Too-many-toes · 10.04

#### Single heel rise test
- **Aim:** tibialis posterior function
- **How:** patient leans on a wall, rises on one tiptoe
- **Positive:** cannot rise, or heel stays in valgus → tibialis posterior failure
- **Why:** tibialis posterior locks the hindfoot so the calf can lift the heel
- **Trap:** test the sound side first (Reider)
- **Video:** [▶ Timonium Foot and Ankle Center · 1:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xV2EoRf0-HE)

[[FIG: Fig 10.21 — Sound side rises, affected cannot · 10.04

#### First metatarsal rise test
- **Aim:** tibialis posterior dysfunction (Reider)
- **How:** patient stands; you rotate the leg outward from behind
- **Positive:** first metatarsal head lifts off the floor → tibialis posterior dysfunction
- **Why:** a weak tendon lets the medial column rise
- **Video:** [▶ Adrián Moro · 0:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DfaELmvSqNU)

[[FIG: Fig 10.22 — First metatarsal head lifts · 10.04

### Is the ankle unstable?
- **Memory:** drawer pulls forward → ATFL; tilt rocks the talus → CFL

#### Anterior drawer test (ankle)
- **Aim:** ATFL laxity
- **How:** patient sits, ankle slightly plantarflexed; you steady the leg, pull the heel forward
- **Positive:** 3–5 mm more than the sound side, soft end point → ATFL torn (Reider)
- **Why:** ATFL stops the talus sliding forward
- **Video:** [▶ The Physio Channel · 0:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XYgt1NWLMPQ)

[[FIG: Fig 10.23 — Heel pulled forward, leg steadied · 10.04

#### Talar tilt (inversion stress) test
- **Aim:** CFL laxity
- **How:** you dorsiflex the ankle to lock it, then invert the heel
- **Positive:** talus rocks into varus, more than the sound side → CFL torn
- **Why:** in dorsiflexion the CFL is tight
- **Video:** [▶ Educom · 0:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ugwWbNXLG4E)

[[FIG: Fig 10.24 — Heel inverted, ankle locked · 10.04

### Is the syndesmosis injured?
#### Squeeze test
- **Aim:** syndesmosis (high ankle) sprain
- **How:** you squeeze tibia and fibula together at mid-calf
- **Positive:** pain at the distal tibiofibular joint → syndesmosis injury
- **Why:** squeezing above springs the bones apart below
- **Video:** [▶ Physical Therapy Nation · 0:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rM9Rk1oucHM)

[[FIG: Fig 10.25 — Squeeze at mid-calf · 10.04

#### External rotation (Kleiger) test
- **Aim:** syndesmosis or deltoid injury
- **How:** patient sits, knee 90°; you steady the leg, rotate the foot outward
- **Positive:** pain over the syndesmosis → syndesmosis; medial pain → deltoid
- **Why:** external rotation wedges the talus between tibia and fibula
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 0:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AXPxMmChQj0)

[[FIG: Fig 10.26 — External rotation stress · 10.04

#### Cotton test
- **Aim:** syndesmosis instability
- **How:** you steady the leg, push the heel and talus sideways
- **Positive:** pain or extra lateral talar shift → tibiofibular separation
- **Why:** a torn syndesmosis lets the mortise widen
- **Video:** [▶ UWEC ATEP · 1:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qX68KET3dls)

[[FIG: Fig 10.27 — Lateral shift of the talus · 10.04

### Is there impingement?
#### Anterolateral impingement test
- **Aim:** synovial (soft-tissue) impingement after sprain
- **How:** thumb presses the anterolateral gutter, foot plantarflexed; then you dorsiflex
- **Positive:** pain worsens on dorsiflexion → synovial impingement
- **Why:** dorsiflexion pinches the trapped synovium
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotherapy UC Copenhagen · 0:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RrooMwP0uVE)

[[FIG: Fig 10.28 — Anterolateral impingement test · 10.04

### Are the peroneal tendons unstable?
#### Peroneal tendon instability test
- **Aim:** subluxing peroneal tendons (torn superior retinaculum) (Reider)
- **How:** patient circles the ankle; you feel behind the lateral malleolus
- **Positive:** tendons snap forward over the malleolus → instability
- **Why:** the retinaculum no longer holds them in the groove
- **Video:** [▶ The Physio Channel · 0:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oPxcpbYNeJ4)

[[FIG: Fig 10.29 — Fingers behind the lateral malleolus · 10.04

### Is a nerve trapped?
#### Tinel sign (tarsal tunnel)
- **Aim:** tarsal tunnel syndrome
- **How:** you tap the tibial nerve behind and below the medial malleolus
- **Positive:** tingling into the sole → tibial nerve compression
- **Why:** an irritable nerve fires when tapped
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 0:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=llHy6kPCEqA)

[[FIG: Fig 10.30 — Tinel over the tarsal tunnel · 10.04

#### Dorsiflexion–eversion test
- **Aim:** tarsal tunnel syndrome
- **How:** you hold the ankle in full dorsiflexion and eversion, toes extended
- **Positive:** symptoms reproduced → tarsal tunnel syndrome
- **Why:** stretches the tibial nerve through the tunnel (Reider)
- **Video:** [▶ Educom · 0:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OMdFP9nwj7g)

[[FIG: Fig 10.31 — Dorsiflexion–eversion test · 10.04

### Is it Morton's neuroma?
#### Metatarsal squeeze (Morton) test
- **Aim:** interdigital (Morton's) neuroma
- **How:** you squeeze the first and fifth metatarsal heads together
- **Positive:** burning pain into the third and fourth toes → neuroma
- **Why:** the heads pinch the nerve in the web space
- **Video:** [▶ MSK Medicine · 0:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BGdfKqMbtac)

[[FIG: Fig 10.32 — Metatarsal heads squeezed · 10.04

#### Mulder click
- **Aim:** confirm Morton's neuroma
- **How:** squeeze the forefoot; press up under the web space
- **Positive:** painful palpable click → neuroma
- **Why:** the swollen nerve pops between the heads
- **Video:** [▶ Educom · 0:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OX7wDLMcczQ)

[[FIG: Fig 10.33 — Squeeze plus web-space pressure · 10.04

### Is it the heel or the big toe?
#### Windlass test
- **Aim:** plantar fasciitis
- **How:** you dorsiflex the big toe fully, ankle neutral
- **Positive:** pain at the plantar fascia origin → plantar fasciitis
- **Why:** toe extension tightens the plantar fascia
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 0:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9r9ei3dCyYs)

[[FIG: Fig 10.34 — Big toe dorsiflexed · 10.04

#### Grind test (first MTP)
- **Aim:** whole-joint arthritis of the first MTP
- **How:** you grasp the big toe, load it and rotate it
- **Positive:** pain and crepitus → hallux rigidus with joint damage
- **Why:** only worn cartilage hurts under load
- **Video:** [▶ Gait Happens · 0:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XxC-6mZKJtc)

10.05.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "two-minute short case"
- "Spot: heel, arch, toes, scars, shoes. Do: tiptoe, the deformity test, one movement."
- "Say: one diagnosis and one differential."

### Tibialis posterior dysfunction (adult flat foot)
- **Spot:** one flat foot, heel valgus, too-many-toes, medial swelling
- **Do:** single heel rise; then flexible or rigid
- **Say:** "Left tibialis posterior dysfunction, stage 2, flexible. Differential: rheumatoid flat foot."

| Stage (Kasr Al-Ainy) | Finding | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | tenosynovitis, no deformity | rest, anti-inflammatory |
| 2 | flexible flat foot | calcaneal osteotomy, FDL transfer |
| 3 | rigid flat foot | arthrodesis |
| 4 | plus ankle valgus | arthrodesis including the ankle |

- FDL = flexor digitorum longus
- **Memory:** 1 sore tendon, 2 flexible flat, 3 rigid flat, 4 ankle too

[[FIG: Fig 10.36 — Flat arch, heel valgus; standing film · 10.05

### Flexible flat foot with hyperlaxity
- **Spot:** young adult, both arches low, high Beighton score
- **Do:** arch forms on tiptoe and with Jack test; Silfverskiöld
- **Say:** "Flexible flat foot with generalised laxity. Differential: accessory navicular."

[[FIG: Fig 10.37 — Low arch from the side · 10.05

### Accessory navicular
- **Spot:** bony bump on the medial midfoot, painful in shoes
- **Do:** tender bump; single heel rise often weak; tiptoe corrects the arch
- **Say:** "Symptomatic accessory navicular, flexible flat foot. Differential: tibialis posterior tendinitis."

[[FIG: Fig 10.38 — Medial bump; ossicle on the film · 10.05

### Pes cavus (cavovarus foot)
- **Spot:** high arch, heel varus, clawed toes, metatarsal head callus
- **Do:** Coleman block; spine, hands, reflexes, sensation
- **Say:** "Bilateral cavovarus feet, likely CMT; flexible heel. Differential: spinal dysraphism."

[[FIG: Fig 10.39 — CMT: cavus foot, clawed hand · 10.05

### Hallux valgus
- **Spot:** big toe drifting out, bunion, crowded second toe
- **Do:** correctable or not; first MTP range; first ray mobility
- **Say:** "Right hallux valgus, correctable, with a painful bunion. Differential: hallux rigidus."

[[FIG: Fig 10.40 — Hallux valgus on the standing film · 10.05

### Hallux rigidus
- **Spot:** dorsal bump on the first MTP, oblique shoe crease
- **Do:** painful, blocked dorsiflexion; grind test
- **Say:** "Left hallux rigidus. Differential: gout of the first MTP."

[[FIG: Fig 10.41 — Advanced hallux rigidus · 10.05

### Neglected equinovarus in the adult
- **Spot:** foot fixed down and in, outer-border callus
- **Do:** passive correction, ankle and subtalar range, sensation, scars
- **Say:** "Neglected rigid equinovarus, post-traumatic. Differential: neglected clubfoot."
- Old deformity → gradual correction, often then fusion (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- Child with clubfoot → ch 11

[[FIG: Fig 10.42 — Post-traumatic equinovarus · 10.05

### Charcot foot
- **Spot:** diabetic, warm swollen foot, rocker-bottom sole, little pain
- **Do:** monofilament, pulses, midfoot ulcer
- **Say:** "Charcot neuroarthropathy of the midfoot. Differential: diabetic foot infection."
- Midfoot is the commonest site (Miller)

[[FIG: Fig 10.43 — Rocker-bottom foot; neuropathic ankle · 10.05

### Chronic Achilles rupture
- **Spot:** missed rupture, flat gait, cannot rise on tiptoe
- **Do:** palpable gap, Thompson, Matles; extra passive dorsiflexion
- **Say:** "Chronic left Achilles rupture. Differential: tendinopathy with partial tear."
- Gap over 5 cm → flexor hallucis longus transfer (Miller)

### Drop foot
- Full case → ch 5 (5.5); gait → ch 1

### Ankle arthritis or malunion
- **Spot:** stiff swollen ankle, old scars
- **Do:** ankle range, then subtalar range; alignment
- **Say:** "Post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the right ankle. Differential: malunion with impingement."

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "present your case"
- "Who, what, how long; standing findings, tests, then supine findings; then diagnosis and stage."
- "Flat foot: say flexible or rigid, and the tibialis posterior stage."

### Present it like this (course case 3)
| Part | Say |
|---|---|
| History | "Ankle and hindfoot pain for 4 years, worse with walking." |
| Standing | "Left heel valgus, mild forefoot abduction." |
| Tests | "On double tiptoe the heel inverts: flexible." |
| Supine | "Tender anterolateral ankle; mild Achilles tightness." |
| Verdict | "Tibialis posterior insufficiency, stage 2; standing films to confirm." |

### Differential of an adult flat foot
| Group | Examples |
|---|---|
| Tendon | tibialis posterior dysfunction |
| Joint | rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis |
| Bone | tarsal coalition, accessory navicular, malunion |
| Nerve | Charcot neuroarthropathy |
| Laxity | flexible flat foot with hyperlaxity |

- **Memory:** tendon, joint, bone, nerve, laxity

### The Examiner Asks
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Normal heel alignment? | 5–10° valgus |
| Toes seen from behind normally? | about one and a half |
| Heel inverts on tiptoe — meaning? | tibialis posterior works, subtalar mobile |
| Why lock the subtalar joint first? | or the midfoot fakes dorsiflexion |
| First thing in a cavus foot? | examine the spine and neurology |
| Coleman corrects the heel — so? | hindfoot flexible, forefoot-driven |
| Can a ruptured Achilles plantarflex? | yes, through the long toe flexors |
| Drawer tests which ligament? | ATFL; talar tilt tests CFL |
| Why dorsiflexion lost after syndesmosis scarring? | the talus is wider in front |
| Most important hallux valgus angle? | first–second intermetatarsal angle |
| Commonest site of Morton's neuroma? | third web space |
| Stage 2 tibialis posterior treatment? | calcaneal osteotomy plus FDL transfer |

| Most important hallux valgus angle? | first–second intermetatarsal angle |
| Commonest site of Morton's neuroma? | third web space |
| Stage 2 tibialis posterior treatment? | calcaneal osteotomy plus FDL transfer |
